summaries.core-syntax: Names, assignment, operators, unpacking, and the small pieces of syntax used throughout Python.
summaries.control-flow: Choose what runs, repeat work, and control whether a loop stops, skips, or continues.
summaries.strings: Create, inspect, split, combine, search, format, encode, and transform text.
summaries.numbers: Work with integers, floating-point values, precise decimals, fractions, and common math operations.
summaries.collections: Store groups of values using lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries, each with different behavior.
summaries.comprehensions: Build collections or lazy generators compactly from other iterables, optionally filtering values.
summaries.functions: Define reusable behavior, control how arguments are accepted, and understand how names are resolved.
summaries.iterators-generators: Understand Python's iteration protocol and produce values lazily instead of building everything at once.
summaries.exceptions: Represent failures explicitly, catch only expected errors, and guarantee cleanup when execution leaves a block.
summaries.oop: Model state and behavior with classes, instances, inheritance, properties, and alternative constructors.
summaries.dataclasses-enum: Reduce class boilerplate for data objects and represent a fixed set of named values.
summaries.dunder-methods: Hook your objects into Python syntax such as printing, comparison, iteration, indexing, and context managers.
summaries.typing: Describe expected value shapes for editors, static type checkers, documentation, and safer refactoring.
summaries.modules-imports: Split code into modules and packages, import public names, and control module execution.
summaries.files-pathlib: Read, write, locate, create, rename, and inspect files and directories safely.
summaries.data-formats: Convert Python values to and from common text or binary formats such as JSON, CSV, TOML, and Base64.
summaries.datetime: Represent dates, times, durations, timestamps, and time zones without losing temporal context.
summaries.stdlib-toolbox: Useful batteries-included data structures and algorithms that often replace custom utility code.
summaries.os-cli: Interact with the operating system, environment variables, command-line arguments, subprocesses, and temporary files.
summaries.logging-debugging: Observe what a program is doing, inspect failures, stop execution interactively, and measure small code paths.
summaries.concurrency: Choose between synchronous code, async I/O, threads, and processes based on what is waiting or consuming CPU.
summaries.testing: Express expected behavior, isolate dependencies, prepare reusable test data, and run focused automated checks.
summaries.sqlite: Use Python's built-in SQLite driver for lightweight relational storage, queries, parameters, and transactions.
summaries.internals-gotchas: Common Python behaviors that cause subtle bugs when object identity, mutation, copying, or evaluation is misunderstood.

core-syntax.print: Display values on standard output, usually for simple program output or debugging.
core-syntax.assign: Bind a name to an object; assignment does not copy the object.
core-syntax.multiple assign: Assign several values to several names in one unpacking statement.
core-syntax.swap: Exchange two values without creating a temporary variable.
core-syntax.augmented: Update a value with an operator such as + or *; mutable objects may change in place.
core-syntax.membership: Check whether a value is contained in a sequence, set, mapping, or other container.
core-syntax.identity: Check whether two references point to the exact same object; most commonly used with None.
core-syntax.walrus: Assign a value inside an expression so you can test it and reuse it immediately.
core-syntax.unpack: Split values from an iterable into separate names; a starred name collects the remainder.
core-syntax.ignore value: Use _ by convention for an unpacked value you intentionally do not need.
core-syntax.delete: Remove a variable binding, collection item, slice, or attribute.
core-syntax.docstring: Attach documentation text to a module, class, function, or method.
core-syntax.numeric separators: Use underscores to make long numeric literals easier to read without changing their value.

control-flow.if / elif / else: Run the first branch whose condition is true, otherwise run the optional else branch.
control-flow.ternary: Choose between two values inside a single expression.
control-flow.for: Take items from an iterable one at a time and run the loop body for each item.
control-flow.while: Repeat a block while its condition remains true.
control-flow.continue: Skip the rest of the current loop iteration and continue with the next one.
control-flow.enumerate: Loop over values while also receiving their index counter.
control-flow.zip: Loop over multiple iterables in parallel, pairing corresponding items.
control-flow.for ... else: Run else only if the loop finishes normally rather than through break.
control-flow.while ... else: Run else only if the condition becomes false rather than the loop ending through break.
control-flow.match: Choose a branch using structural pattern matching instead of many comparisons.
control-flow.match guard: Add an extra boolean condition to a matched case.
control-flow.wildcard case: Match any value not handled by an earlier case.

strings.index / slice: Read one character or part of a string; negative indexes count from the end and [::-1] reverses it.
strings.strip: Remove whitespace from both ends; lstrip and rstrip remove it from only one side.
strings.split: Break text into a list using a separator, or split it by line boundaries.
strings.join: Combine strings using the string before .join() as the separator.
strings.replace: Return a new string with matching text replaced; strings themselves are immutable.
strings.find: Find the first match position; find returns -1 when missing, while index raises ValueError.
strings.prefix / suffix: Check whether text starts or ends with a specific string.
strings.f-string: Insert values or expressions directly into text; :.2f formats a number to two decimal places.
strings.case: Change letter case; casefold is the stronger choice for case-insensitive comparisons.
strings.tests: Check whether the whole string consists of digits, letters, whitespace, or another character class.
strings.partition: Split once around a separator and always return head, separator, and tail.
strings.padding: Align text to a width or pad numeric text with leading zeroes.
strings.encode / decode: Convert text to bytes with an encoding, or bytes back to text using the same encoding.
strings.raw string: Treat backslashes mostly as literal characters, which is useful for paths and regular expressions.

numbers.numeric types: Use int for whole numbers, float for binary floating point, and complex for real-plus-imaginary values.
numbers.division: / returns true division, // floors the quotient, and % returns the remainder.
numbers.power: Raise a value to a power with ** or pow().
numbers.abs / round: Get a magnitude with abs(), or round a number to a requested precision.
numbers.divmod: Compute quotient and remainder together in one operation.
numbers.bases: Convert integers to binary/octal/hex text, or parse text using a specific numeric base.
numbers.math: Use common mathematical functions such as square root, ceiling, and floor.
numbers.isclose: Compare floating-point values using a tolerance instead of exact equality.
numbers.constants: Use standard mathematical and special floating-point constants such as pi, infinity, and NaN.
numbers.Decimal: Represent base-10 decimal values precisely for money or other decimal-sensitive calculations.
numbers.Fraction: Represent an exact rational number as numerator and denominator.
numbers.complex parts: Read the real/imaginary components of a complex number or compute its conjugate.
numbers.clamp pattern: Restrict a value so it stays between a lower and upper bound.

collections.list: Ordered, mutable sequence whose items can be added, removed, replaced, or reordered.
collections.append / extend: append adds one item; extend adds every item from another iterable.
collections.insert / pop: Insert an item at a position, or remove and return an item from a position.
collections.sort: list.sort() mutates a list; sorted() returns a new sorted list from any iterable.
collections.tuple: Ordered, immutable sequence; a one-item tuple needs a trailing comma.
collections.set: Mutable collection of unique hashable values, useful for membership tests and deduplication.
collections.set ops: Compute union, intersection, difference, or symmetric difference between sets.
collections.dict: Mutable mapping from unique hashable keys to values.
collections.dict get: Read a mapping value without raising KeyError when the key is absent.
collections.dict iterate: Iterate through dictionary keys and values together.
collections.dict update: Add or overwrite multiple dictionary entries from another mapping.
collections.dict merge: Create a merged dictionary with |, or update the left dictionary in place with |=.
collections.dict remove: Remove a key with pop or del; pop can provide a safe default for missing keys.
collections.setdefault: Return an existing value or insert a default value, often useful when grouping items.
collections.frozenset: Immutable set that can itself be used as a dictionary key or set member.
collections.copy: Create a shallow copy of a list or dictionary; nested objects remain shared.

comprehensions.list comp: Build a new list by transforming each item from an iterable.
comprehensions.filter: Build a list containing only items that satisfy a condition.
comprehensions.transform + filter: Filter input items and transform the ones that remain in one expression.
comprehensions.set comp: Build a set from transformed items, automatically keeping only unique values.
comprehensions.dict comp: Build a dictionary by computing each key and value.
comprehensions.generator expr: Create values lazily instead of building the entire collection in memory.
comprehensions.conditional value: Choose between two output values for every item inside a comprehension.
comprehensions.flatten one level: Flatten one nested iterable level into a single list.
comprehensions.nested pairs: Produce every combination of items from two iterables.
comprehensions.any: Return True as soon as at least one generated condition is true.
comprehensions.all: Return True only if every generated condition is true.
comprehensions.sum: Add values produced lazily from an iterable or generator expression.

functions.define: Create a reusable callable with named parameters and a return value.
functions.default arg: Use a fallback argument when the caller omits it; avoid mutable objects as defaults.
functions.*args: Collect extra positional arguments into a tuple.
functions.**kwargs: Collect extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.
functions.keyword-only: Require arguments after * to be passed by name.
functions.positional-only: Require arguments before / to be passed by position.
functions.unpack call: Expand an iterable into positional arguments and a mapping into keyword arguments.
functions.lambda: Create a small anonymous single-expression function, often used as a key or callback.
functions.annotation: Describe intended parameter and return types for tools and readers; annotations do not enforce types by themselves.
functions.multiple return: Return one tuple containing several values that the caller can unpack.
functions.LEGB: Python resolves a name through Local, Enclosing, Global, then Builtins scopes.
functions.global: Rebind a module-level name from inside a function.
functions.nonlocal: Rebind a name from the nearest enclosing function scope.
functions.first-class function: Functions are objects, so they can be stored, passed as arguments, and returned.

iterators-generators.iterator: Stateful object that produces one value at a time until it is exhausted.
iterators-generators.next: Request the next iterator value; without a default, exhaustion raises StopIteration.
iterators-generators.generator: Function containing yield; calling it creates a lazy iterator that preserves state between values.
iterators-generators.yield from: Delegate yielding to another iterable or generator.
iterators-generators.generator expr: Create a lazy iterator with comprehension-like syntax.
iterators-generators.chain: Treat several iterables as one continuous sequence without copying their contents.
iterators-generators.islice: Take a slice-like window from an iterator without first converting it to a list.
iterators-generators.count / cycle: Create an unbounded counter or endlessly repeat an iterable; the consumer must decide when to stop.
iterators-generators.repeat: Yield the same value repeatedly, optionally for a fixed number of times.
iterators-generators.takewhile: Yield items while a predicate remains true, then stop at the first false result.
iterators-generators.dropwhile: Skip items while a predicate is true, then yield the rest.
iterators-generators.tee: Create independent iterator views backed by buffering; large consumption differences can use memory.
iterators-generators.generator send: Resume a generator while injecting a value into its suspended yield expression.
iterators-generators.close: Stop a generator early by raising GeneratorExit inside it.

exceptions.try / except: Run code that may fail and handle a specific expected exception.
exceptions.multiple types: Handle several exception types with the same recovery logic.
exceptions.else: Run code only when the try block completed without an exception.
exceptions.finally: Run cleanup code whether the try block succeeds, fails, returns, or exits a loop.
exceptions.raise: Create or propagate an exception deliberately when an operation cannot continue correctly.
exceptions.re-raise: Propagate the currently handled exception unchanged after logging or partial handling.
exceptions.cause: Wrap a lower-level exception while preserving it as the explicit cause.
exceptions.custom error: Create an exception type that expresses a failure meaningful to your application.
exceptions.suppress: Intentionally ignore only named exception types inside a small explicit block.
exceptions.exception notes: Attach extra diagnostic context to an exception before it propagates.
exceptions.ExceptionGroup: Carry multiple exceptions together, commonly when concurrent operations fail.
exceptions.except*: Handle matching exceptions inside an ExceptionGroup while unmatched ones continue to propagate.
exceptions.cleanup: Prefer context managers for resources so cleanup happens reliably on every exit path.

oop.class: Define a type that groups state and behavior for its instances.
oop.constructor: Initialize a newly created instance; self is the instance being initialized.
oop.instance method: Define behavior that receives the instance as its first argument.
oop.inheritance: Create a subclass that reuses and can override behavior from a base class.
oop.super: Call the next implementation in the method-resolution order, usually a base-class method.
oop.property: Expose method-backed behavior through normal attribute syntax.
oop.class method: Define a method that receives the class as cls, often for alternate constructors.
oop.static method: Namespace a function inside a class without automatically receiving self or cls.
oop.isinstance: Check whether an object is an instance of a class or any of its subclasses.
oop.issubclass: Check whether one class derives from another.
oop.MRO: Inspect the order Python follows when looking up methods across an inheritance hierarchy.
oop.slots: Declare expected instance attributes and usually avoid a per-instance __dict__.
oop.name mangling: Rename double-underscore attributes internally to reduce accidental subclass collisions, not to provide real privacy.
oop.composition: Build behavior by storing collaborating objects instead of inheriting from them.

dataclasses-enum.dataclass: Generate common data-object methods such as __init__ and __repr__ from annotated fields.
dataclasses-enum.default factory: Create a fresh default object for each dataclass instance, avoiding shared mutable defaults.
dataclasses-enum.frozen: Prevent normal field reassignment after a dataclass instance is created.
dataclasses-enum.slots: Generate a slotted dataclass with a fixed attribute layout and usually lower memory overhead.
dataclasses-enum.asdict: Convert a dataclass instance recursively into standard dictionaries and collections.
dataclasses-enum.replace: Create a new dataclass instance with selected fields changed.
dataclasses-enum.Enum: Define a fixed set of named values with identity and readable names.
dataclasses-enum.auto: Let Enum generate member values automatically.
dataclasses-enum.StrEnum: Create enum members that also behave like strings.
dataclasses-enum.IntEnum: Create enum members that also behave like integers.
dataclasses-enum.enum by name: Look up an enum member using its member name.
dataclasses-enum.enum by value: Look up the enum member whose stored value matches the provided value.
dataclasses-enum.post init: Run custom validation or derived-field setup after the generated dataclass initializer.

dunder-methods.representation: Control developer-oriented repr() output and user-oriented str() output.
dunder-methods.iteration: Make an object iterable and, for iterators, define how the next item is produced.
dunder-methods.membership: Customize the behavior of value in obj.
dunder-methods.indexing: Customize reading or assigning values with square-bracket syntax.
dunder-methods.callable object: Allow an instance to be called like a function.
dunder-methods.comparison: Customize equality and ordering operators for your objects.
dunder-methods.hashing: Define a stable hash so compatible immutable objects can be dictionary keys or set members.
dunder-methods.context manager: Control setup and cleanup for synchronous with blocks.
dunder-methods.async context: Control setup and cleanup for async with blocks.
dunder-methods.arithmetic: Customize arithmetic operators such as +, -, and *.
dunder-methods.attribute fallback: Compute or provide an attribute only after normal attribute lookup fails.
dunder-methods.new instance: Customize object creation before __init__ runs; most classes do not need to override it.
dunder-methods.formatting: Customize how format(obj, spec) and f-string format specifications render an object.

typing.annotation: Attach an expected type to a name for readers, editors, and static type checkers.
typing.union: Allow a value to have any one of several declared types.
typing.optional: Allow either the declared value type or None.
typing.collections: Describe element types inside generic collections such as lists and dictionaries.
typing.tuple: Describe the type of each position in a tuple.
typing.Callable: Describe the parameter types and return type of a callable.
typing.Literal: Restrict a value to specific literal choices during static checking.
typing.type alias: Give a reusable name to a type expression so annotations stay readable.
typing.TypeVar: Represent a type variable that connects types across parameters and return values.
typing.generic syntax: Define a class or function that works consistently with a parameterized type.
typing.Protocol: Describe required behavior structurally: a value matches if it provides the required members.
typing.TypedDict: Describe the expected keys and value types of dictionary-shaped data.
typing.Self: Express that a method returns the same concrete class as the receiver.
typing.Final: Tell type checkers that a name should not be reassigned or overridden.
typing.ClassVar: Mark an annotation as class-level state rather than an instance field.
typing.cast: Tell the type checker to treat a value as a type; it does not convert the runtime object.

modules-imports.import: Load a module and bind its module object to a name.
modules-imports.alias: Bind an imported module to a shorter or clearer local name.
modules-imports.from import: Import selected names directly into the current namespace.
modules-imports.import alias: Import one selected object under a different local name.
modules-imports.relative import: Import from the current package using dots to express relative package location.
modules-imports.main guard: Run code only when the file is executed as the entry module, not when it is imported.
modules-imports.public API: Declare the names intended for wildcard export and document the module's public surface.
modules-imports.run module: Execute a module through Python's module loader while preserving package import behavior.
modules-imports.reload: Re-execute an already imported module object; existing external references may still point to old objects.
modules-imports.dynamic import: Import a module when its name is only known at runtime.
modules-imports.module path: Inspect the source-file path associated with a module when one exists.
modules-imports.package name: Inspect the package context Python uses for relative imports.
modules-imports.search path: Inspect or modify the directories Python searches when resolving imports.

files-pathlib.read text: Read an entire text file into a string using the requested character encoding.
files-pathlib.write text: Write a complete string to a text file and return the number of characters written.
files-pathlib.open safely: Open a file inside a context manager so it is closed even if an error occurs.
files-pathlib.binary mode: Read raw bytes instead of decoded text.
files-pathlib.join path: Combine path components using Path semantics instead of manual separators.
files-pathlib.exists / type: Check whether a path exists and whether it represents a file or directory.
files-pathlib.glob: Find paths matching a filename pattern; rglob searches recursively.
files-pathlib.mkdir: Create a directory, optionally creating missing parents and tolerating an existing directory.
files-pathlib.rename: Move or rename a filesystem path.
files-pathlib.unlink: Delete a file or symbolic link, optionally ignoring a missing path.
files-pathlib.parts: Read common path components such as file name, stem, suffix, and parent directory.
files-pathlib.resolve: Produce an absolute normalized path and resolve symbolic links where supported.
files-pathlib.iterate lines: Stream a text file line by line instead of reading the entire file at once.
files-pathlib.seek / tell: Move the file position or inspect the current byte/stream position.

data-formats.JSON parse: Convert JSON text into Python dictionaries, lists, numbers, strings, booleans, and None.
data-formats.JSON serialize: Convert compatible Python values into JSON text.
data-formats.JSON file: Read JSON directly from a file object or write Python data directly to one.
data-formats.CSV rows: Read or write CSV data as sequences of column values.
data-formats.CSV dicts: Read or write CSV rows using column names as dictionary keys.
data-formats.TOML: Parse TOML configuration data with Python's built-in tomllib reader.
data-formats.INI: Create a parser for INI-style section/key configuration files.
data-formats.pickle: Serialize and restore Python-specific objects; use only with trusted data.
data-formats.pickle safety: Never unpickle untrusted input because loading can execute arbitrary code.
data-formats.struct pack: Encode numeric values into fixed-layout binary bytes using a format string.
data-formats.struct unpack: Decode fixed-layout binary bytes back into Python values.
data-formats.base64: Encode binary data as Base64 bytes or decode Base64 back to the original bytes.
data-formats.YAML: Parse YAML with a third-party library; use safe_load for untrusted or ordinary configuration data.

datetime.today: Return the current local calendar date without a time component.
datetime.UTC now: Return the current time as a timezone-aware UTC datetime.
datetime.duration: Represent a span of time that can be added to or subtracted from dates and datetimes.
datetime.parse: Convert text matching an explicit format pattern into a datetime.
datetime.format: Convert a datetime into formatted text using strftime directives.
datetime.ISO parse: Parse an ISO-8601-style date/time string into a datetime.
datetime.ISO format: Serialize a date or datetime to an ISO-8601-style string.
datetime.timezone: Load an IANA time zone with real daylight-saving and historical offset rules.
datetime.timestamp → datetime: Convert a Unix timestamp into a timezone-aware datetime.
datetime.datetime → timestamp: Convert a datetime to seconds since the Unix epoch.
datetime.attach timezone: Assign timezone metadata without changing the displayed clock time; use only when the naive time is already known to be in that zone.
datetime.convert timezone: Convert an aware datetime to another zone while preserving the same instant.
datetime.combine: Combine a separate date and time value into one datetime.

stdlib-toolbox.Counter: Count occurrences of hashable items and retrieve the most common values.
stdlib-toolbox.defaultdict: Create a dictionary that automatically supplies a default value for missing keys.
stdlib-toolbox.deque: Use a double-ended queue with efficient appends and pops from both ends.
stdlib-toolbox.cache: Memoize all calls by arguments with an unbounded function cache.
stdlib-toolbox.LRU cache: Memoize recent calls while limiting how many argument/result pairs are retained.
stdlib-toolbox.partial: Create a new callable with some arguments pre-filled.
stdlib-toolbox.heap: Maintain a min-heap so the smallest item can be pushed and popped efficiently.
stdlib-toolbox.bisect: Insert or search in a sorted list while preserving its sort order.
stdlib-toolbox.product: Generate the Cartesian product of multiple iterables.
stdlib-toolbox.permutations: Generate ordered arrangements of items without repetition.
stdlib-toolbox.combinations: Generate unordered selections of items without repetition.
stdlib-toolbox.statistics: Compute common descriptive statistics such as mean and median.
stdlib-toolbox.random: Choose or shuffle pseudo-random values; do not use it for security-sensitive randomness.
stdlib-toolbox.secrets: Generate cryptographically strong random tokens for passwords, links, or secrets.
stdlib-toolbox.wraps: Preserve the wrapped function's name, documentation, and metadata when writing decorators.

os-cli.cwd: Read or change the process's current working directory.
os-cli.environment: Read environment variables or access the environment mapping directly.
os-cli.CLI args: Read the raw command-line arguments passed to the Python process.
os-cli.exit: Stop the program intentionally with a process exit status.
os-cli.run command: Run an external command and optionally fail immediately when its exit code is non-zero.
os-cli.capture output: Run a command while capturing stdout/stderr as text instead of printing it.
os-cli.copy / move: Copy file metadata-preserving content or move files/directories to another path.
os-cli.temporary dir: Create a temporary directory that is automatically removed when the context exits.
os-cli.argparse: Define and parse structured command-line options and arguments.
os-cli.which: Find the executable path that would be used for a command on the current PATH.
os-cli.platform: Inspect the current operating system or runtime platform.
os-cli.stdin / stdout: Access the process's standard input, output, and error streams directly.
os-cli.walk tree: Traverse a directory tree and receive each directory with its child directories and files.

logging-debugging.basic config: Configure a simple root logging setup, typically once near program startup.
logging-debugging.logger: Create or retrieve a named logger, usually using the module name.
logging-debugging.levels: Write messages with severity levels from detailed debugging through errors.
logging-debugging.exception: Log a message together with the current exception traceback from inside an except block.
logging-debugging.breakpoint: Pause execution and enter the configured interactive debugger.
logging-debugging.pdb: Run a script under Python's built-in command-line debugger.
logging-debugging.traceback: Print the traceback for the exception currently being handled.
logging-debugging.timeit: Measure execution time repeatedly for a small code snippet or callable.
logging-debugging.assert invariant: Fail fast when an internal assumption is false; assertions can be disabled and are not input validation.
logging-debugging.inspect signature: Inspect a callable's declared parameters and return annotation.
logging-debugging.caller stack: Capture the current call stack as formatted text for diagnostics.
logging-debugging.warning: Emit a runtime warning that callers can filter, display, or promote to an error.
logging-debugging.logger format: Define which metadata fields appear in each formatted log record.

concurrency.async function: Define a coroutine function; calling it creates a coroutine that must be awaited or scheduled.
concurrency.await: Pause the current coroutine until another awaitable completes while allowing the event loop to run other work.
concurrency.run event loop: Start an event loop, run the top-level coroutine, and cleanly shut the loop down.
concurrency.create task: Schedule a coroutine to run concurrently on the current event loop.
concurrency.gather: Wait for several awaitables and return their results in input order.
concurrency.TaskGroup: Run related async tasks as one structured unit and propagate failures together.
concurrency.thread pool: Use operating-system threads, typically for blocking I/O or code that releases the GIL.
concurrency.process pool: Use separate processes for CPU-heavy Python work that benefits from true parallel execution.
concurrency.timeout: Limit how long an async block may wait before cancellation is triggered.
concurrency.sleep: Suspend a coroutine without blocking the event loop.
concurrency.queue: Coordinate async producers and consumers without manually sharing a plain list.
concurrency.lock: Allow only one coroutine at a time into a protected async critical section.
concurrency.thread: Start one operating-system thread running a target function.
concurrency.to_thread: Run a blocking synchronous function in a worker thread while keeping an async calling interface.

testing.assert: Fail the current test when the expected condition is false.
testing.unittest case: Create a unittest test class whose methods define individual test cases.
testing.unittest equality: Assert that two values compare equal using unittest's diagnostic output.
testing.mock: Create a controllable test double that records calls and can return configured values.
testing.patch: Temporarily replace the name used by code under test and restore it automatically afterward.
testing.pytest test: Define a pytest test as a normal function whose failures are reported from assertions/exceptions.
testing.pytest fixture: Provide reusable setup or test data through pytest dependency injection by parameter name.
testing.pytest raises: Assert that a block raises the expected exception type.
testing.parametrize: Run one pytest test repeatedly with different input and expected-value combinations.
testing.monkeypatch: Temporarily change environment variables, attributes, mappings, or paths for a test.
testing.tmp_path: Receive a unique temporary Path directory for filesystem tests.
testing.approx: Compare floating-point values using an appropriate tolerance instead of exact equality.
testing.unittest subTest: Run several related checks inside one unittest method while reporting each case separately.
testing.run pytest: Run the full suite quietly or target one specific test by node id.

sqlite.connect: Open a SQLite database file and return a connection object.
sqlite.execute: Execute one SQL statement through a connection or cursor.
sqlite.parameters: Bind values separately from SQL text to avoid quoting bugs and SQL injection.
sqlite.fetch one: Return the next result row, or None when no rows remain.
sqlite.fetch all: Load all remaining result rows into a list.
sqlite.transaction: Use the connection as a context manager so successful work commits and exceptions roll back.
sqlite.row mapping: Return rows that support both index access and column-name access.
sqlite.insert many: Execute one parameterized statement repeatedly for many rows of values.
sqlite.commit: Persist the current transaction's changes to the database.
sqlite.rollback: Discard uncommitted changes in the current transaction.
sqlite.last inserted id: Read the row id generated by the most recent insert on that cursor.
sqlite.memory DB: Create a temporary SQLite database stored only in memory for fast tests or scratch work.
sqlite.close: Release the database connection explicitly when it is no longer needed.

internals-gotchas.mutable default: A mutable default is created once when the function is defined, so calls can accidentally share state.
internals-gotchas.late binding: Closures normally read captured names when called, not when the closure was created.
internals-gotchas.identity vs equality: is asks whether two references are the same object; == asks whether their values compare equal.
internals-gotchas.shallow copy: Copy only the outer object; nested objects are still shared.
internals-gotchas.deep copy: Recursively copy nested state, which is more independent but can be expensive or inappropriate.
internals-gotchas.truthiness: Conditions accept any value; Python converts it using truth-value rules instead of requiring a literal bool.
internals-gotchas.hashability: Dictionary keys and set members need stable hash/equality behavior.
internals-gotchas.iterator exhaustion: Most iterators are one-pass; once consumed, they do not restart automatically.
internals-gotchas.aliasing: Assignment can give one object several names, so mutation through one name is visible through the others.
internals-gotchas.nested list trap: Multiplying a nested list can duplicate references to the same inner list; build each row separately.
internals-gotchas.sort return: list.sort() changes the list in place and deliberately returns None.
internals-gotchas.dict order: Dictionaries preserve insertion order, so iteration follows the order keys were added.
internals-gotchas.floating point: Binary floating-point values may not represent decimal fractions exactly; compare approximately when appropriate.
internals-gotchas.encoding: Specify a text encoding explicitly so file behavior is predictable across machines.

theoryCards.title: Mutability & References
theoryCards.summary: The key mental model: variables are names bound to objects. Mutation changes an object; assignment changes what a name points to.

entries.meaning: The object can change in place, so every reference to that same object observes the change.
entries.detail: list · dict · set · most class instances

entries.meaning: The object itself cannot change in place; an apparent update creates another value and rebinds a name.
entries.detail: int · float · bool · str · tuple · frozenset · bytes

entries.meaning: Assignment points a name at an object. It does not clone the object.
Two names can refer to the same mutable object, so mutation through one name is visible through the other.
entries.detail: b = a · b.append(1) · a also changed

entries.meaning: Rebinding changes which object a name refers to; mutation changes the existing object itself.
Parameters are new local names bound to the caller's objects; mutating a passed mutable object can affect caller-visible state.
Create a new outer container while keeping references to the same nested objects.
Recursively copy nested state when the new structure really must be independent.

more.meaning: A tuple cannot replace its own elements, but an element may itself be a mutable object that can still change.
+= may mutate a mutable object such as a list, while immutable values such as strings produce a new object.
Function default objects are created once, so a mutable default can leak state between calls.
more.detail: def f(items=None): items = [] if items is None else items

more.meaning: For known simple shapes, copy the levels you need instead of automatically deep-copying everything.
id() identifies an object for its lifetime in the current process; it is useful for understanding aliasing, not business identity.

theoryCards.title: Identity, Hashing & Truthiness
theoryCards.summary: Three related rules decide how values compare, whether they can be keys, and how they behave inside conditions.

entries.meaning: Compare values using equality semantics, which classes can customize with __eq__.
Check whether both references point to the exact same object. Prefer it for None and unique sentinels.
A value has stable hash/equality behavior and may be used as a dictionary key or set member.
entries.detail: str · int · frozenset · tuple of hashable values

entries.meaning: Common mutable containers are deliberately unhashable because changing them would break hash-based lookup.
Conditions ask for a value's truth value; values are not required to literally be True or False.
None, false booleans, numeric zero, and empty containers/text evaluate as false.
Boolean operators short-circuit and return one of their operands, which makes fallback expressions possible.
Convert a value to its truth value and negate it, producing a real bool.

more.meaning: A class can define __bool__, or fall back to __len__, to control whether its instances are truthy.
Objects that compare equal must produce the same hash; mutable equality state therefore makes unsafe keys.
Use a unique object when None is a valid input and you need to distinguish 'missing' from 'explicitly None'.
Python can express range-style comparisons directly without repeating the middle operand.
Membership usually uses container-specific lookup or equality semantics, not object identity.
